newsitem.title: GERMANY: Protests break out in Europe over modified grain.
newsitem.headline: Protests break out in Europe over modified grain.

text.p: Protestors staged three demonstrations in Europe on Thursday against genetically- engineered feed grains that environmental activists say could threaten human health.
Police broke up two -- in Hamburg and on the Rhine -- while a third in the Netherlands was due to end by nightfall.

Swiss authorities said they would impound a Rhine barge that Greenpeace activists had tried for hours to prevent from entering Switzerland, claiming it was was illegally importing genetically modified soybeans.
"This is OK for us now," Greenpeace spokesman Stefan Weber said. "The prosecutor has said he would see what was happening with the cargo."
A spokesman for Basle prosecutors confirmed they would temporarily seize the barge once it crossed into Swiss waters from Germany, then release it once its cargo was impounded.
Genetically altered soybeans are not allowed as food or fodder in Switzerland, a spokeswoman for the Federal Health Office said. They can be imported only for re-export.

A dozen Greenpeace activists had earlier secured the barge to a jetty in the town of Weil, downriver from the Swiss border at Basel, and chained themselves on board. Police ejected them, but protesters in rubber rafts halted the barge again.
The Dutch soybean protest took place at Zwijndrecht, near Rotterdam, where environmental group Milieudefensie, an affiliate of Friends of the Earth, blockaded a Unilever plant.
"We are demanding the labelling of products containing gene-soya," Milieudefensie spokesman Victor van den Belt said.
He said some 50 activists were blocking the delivery entrance to the Unimills plant which processes edible oils including soyoil for use in Unilever products such as margarine.
A Unilever spokesman said management had spoken to them and promised to pass on their concerns to Unilever top management.
But he added Unilever's stance on the issue had not changed.
"The company doesn't see any reason not to use this soya in its products, it's perfectly safe," he said.
In Hamburg, police dispersed a Greenpeace demonstration against maize going to the Czech Republic.
The Hamburg demonstration had been aimed at stopping the loading of maize onto trains bound for the Czech Republic.
"Police are clearing the site and loading will continue," said Hans-Herbert Kathke of Neuhof Hafengesellschaft mbH, the company handling the 33,000 tonne cargo.
The cargo on the ship Huta Katowice, orginating in the U.S, was believed to contain modified maize, which is not yet allowed to be imported into the European Union.
The EU Commission is due to decide on December 18 whether to allow imports of such modified maize.
Until then, it is illegal to market it in the EU, but Greenpeace says cargoes may have reached Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain and Portugal.
Greenpeace fears an antibiotic resistant gene inserted into the maize could be transferred to animals and so find its way into the human food chain.
The new type of soybean attacked by activists was developed by U.S. chemicals group Monsanto to be resistant to its own new "super weedkiller" Roundup.

Environmental groups describe the Roundup technology as a risky experiment with nature although the Monsanto strain of bean has been given a clean bill of health by U.S. and EU authorities, who say it poses no danger to the human food chain.
